govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AutopsyCommonEr: Government material filed under the heading Autopsy Common Errors makes up this document, a technical piece on the mistakes that can occur in autopsy procedure. It sits in the archive among the Kennedy assassination files, where the quality of President Kennedy's autopsy has been argued over for decades. Outside works on autopsy practice were collected there as reference. The document is kept as issued, for readers of the forensic literature around the case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GentileGMarvinC: nsia-GentileGMarvinCIA Gentile G Marvin CIA: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KRTN-Knight-Rid:
Researchers kept a key to their own shorthand: an abbreviation key for newspaper and research sources. The key covers Warren Commission exhibits, cited everywhere by number. It also reaches Mae Brussell's research files, the vast private archive of the California investigator.

Anyone who has opened a researcher's notes knows the problem this solves. Citations shrink to initials and codes that die with their maker. A key preserves the codebook, so later readers can expand every reference and follow the trail. It is a small tool that keeps a whole archive legible.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LittellFranklin:
An unnamed writer sent this letter on June 30, 1968, to Frank Wright of the Freedom Institute. In it, the writer identifies himself as the author of the first critical analysis of the Warren Report. His signature cannot be recovered from the text, so the claim stands without a name attached.

The Warren Report had been attacked in print almost from the day it appeared, in 1964. Several early critics competed for the standing of having doubted it first. The letter preserves one such claim, made privately to a sympathetic reader four years later. It is a small artifact of the credit and rivalry inside the first generation of assassination research.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MannThomasCAmba:
A magazine profile titled 'One Mann & 20 Problems' introduces Thomas Clifton Mann in a new job. Mann had become assistant secretary of state for inter-American affairs. He was also President Johnson's top policymaker for Latin America. The headline promises one official facing a hemisphere's worth of troubles. The publication and the author are not identified in the file.

Mann was a career diplomat with long service in Latin America. The profile belongs to the moment he took charge of the region's policy under Johnson. It presents the man, his record, and the problems queued on his desk. As evidence, it shows how a new policymaker was sold to magazine readers: experience first, then the list of crises.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PinkertonJoseph:
Andrew Gordon wrote this article about a San Francisco Spiritualist minister. The minister claims that John F. Kennedy was 'totally psychic.' In his account, Kennedy used his psychic powers to guide America. The piece is filed under the name of the Reverend Joseph J. Pinkerton.

Spiritualist claims about famous men were a steady magazine genre. A president who could be cast as a secret seer made good copy, and Kennedy's death gave such claims a market. Gordon reports the minister's case in the minister's own terms. The article is not evidence about Kennedy. It is evidence about the culture around him: the psychics, ministers, and editors who kept his name working in print long after Dallas.
